questions.q: In the Watson-Crick model of DNA, adenine pairs with thymine by:
questions.solution:
**A pairs with T by two hydrogen bonds**; G pairs with C by **three**.

This is why a GC-rich region has a **higher melting temperature** — more bonds must be broken to separate the strands.

Note the pairing is always **purine with pyrimidine**, which keeps the width of the helix constant at $2\ \text{nm}$ along its whole length.

questions.q: DNA replication is described as semi-conservative because:
options: Each daughter molecule has one parental and one new strand
questions.solution:
Each daughter molecule keeps **one parental strand** and gains **one newly synthesised** strand.

The parental strand acts as the template, so the information is conserved exactly.

This was proved by **Meselson and Stahl** in 1958, using heavy nitrogen $^{15}\text{N}$ and density-gradient centrifugation — the first generation gave a single intermediate band, which ruled out conservative replication, and the second gave two bands, which ruled out dispersive.

questions.q: The enzyme that synthesises RNA from a DNA template is:
questions.solution:
**RNA polymerase** carries out transcription, reading the template strand $3'\to5'$ and building RNA $5'\to3'$.

Unlike DNA polymerase it needs **no primer** — it can start a chain from nothing, which is one reason primers for DNA replication are made of RNA.

It also lacks proofreading, so transcription is less accurate than replication — tolerable, because a faulty transcript is discarded rather than inherited.

questions.q: The genetic code is said to be **degenerate** because:
options: Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon
One codon codes for many amino acids
It is different in every species
questions.solution:
**Degeneracy** means most amino acids are specified by **more than one codon** — there are 64 codons for 20 amino acids.

Crucially, the code is still **unambiguous**: each codon specifies exactly one amino acid. Degeneracy runs one way only.

The redundancy is mostly in the **third base**, which is why many third-position mutations are silent — a built-in buffer against mutation.

Hershey and Chase used bacteriophages with **radioactive labels**: $^{32}\text{P}$ for DNA (protein has no phosphorus) and $^{35}\text{S}$ for protein (DNA has no sulphur).

After infection, only $^{32}\text{P}$ entered the bacteria and appeared in the progeny phages. The $^{35}\text{S}$ stayed outside in the discarded coats.

So **DNA is the genetic material**. The elegance is in the choice of labels: each element is present in one molecule and absent from the other, so the result cannot be ambiguous.

questions.q: In the lac operon, the repressor protein binds to the:
questions.solution:
The repressor binds the **operator**, a short sequence between the promoter and the structural genes.

Bound there, it physically blocks RNA polymerase from moving forward, so transcription is switched **off**.

When lactose is present, its isomer **allolactose** acts as the inducer: it binds the repressor, changes its shape, and the repressor falls off the operator — switching the operon **on**. This is **negative regulation**, since the default state is off.

questions.q: The initiation codon in the genetic code is:
questions.solution:
**AUG** is the start codon, and it also codes for **methionine** — so every newly made polypeptide begins with methionine, often removed later.

The three **stop** codons are UAA, UAG and UGA. They code for no amino acid and have no tRNA; translation ends when a release factor binds them.

questions.q: The two strands of DNA are described as antiparallel, meaning:
questions.solution:
**Antiparallel** means one strand runs $5'\to3'$ while its partner runs $3'\to5'$.

This has a real consequence at the replication fork. DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to a $3'$ end, so it synthesises in one direction only. One strand is therefore made **continuously** (the leading strand) and the other in short **Okazaki fragments** (the lagging strand), later joined by ligase.

The awkwardness of lagging-strand synthesis is entirely a consequence of antiparallelism.

questions.q: Approximately how many genes were found in the human genome?
questions.solution:
About **20,000 to 25,000** protein-coding genes — a considerable surprise, since estimates before the project ran to 100,000.

The $3$ billion figure is the number of **base pairs**, not genes.

The low count means complexity cannot come from gene number alone. It comes from **alternative splicing**, post-translational modification and regulation, so one gene can yield many proteins.

questions.q: A double-stranded DNA molecule contains $30\%$ adenine. What percentage of guanine does it contain?
questions.solution:
By **Chargaff's rules**, $A = T$ and $G = C$.

If $A = 30\%$ then $T = 30\%$, so together they are $60\%$.

The remaining $40\%$ is shared equally between G and C:

$G = \dfrac{40}{2} = \mathbf{20\%}$

questions.q: How many codons are there in the genetic code?
questions.solution:
A codon is three bases, and each position can be any of four bases.

$4^{3} = \mathbf{64}$ codons.

Of these, 61 specify amino acids and 3 are stop codons.

questions.q: An mRNA has 300 nucleotides in its coding sequence, including the stop codon. How many amino acids are in the resulting polypeptide?
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{300}{3} = 100$ codons in total.

The **stop codon codes for no amino acid**, so it must be subtracted:

$100 - 1 = \mathbf{99}$ amino acids.

Forgetting the stop codon and answering 100 is the usual error.

questions.q: How many base pairs are there in one complete turn of the B-form DNA double helix?
questions.solution:
One full turn of B-DNA spans about $3.4\ \text{nm}$ and contains roughly $\mathbf{10}$ base pairs, so consecutive pairs are $0.34\ \text{nm}$ apart.

The measured value is closer to 10.5, but 10 is the figure normally quoted.

questions.q: Approximately how many base pairs, in billions, are there in the human genome?
questions.solution:
About $\mathbf{3}$ billion base pairs, roughly $3.2\times10^{9}$.

Remarkably, less than $2\%$ of it codes for protein. Much of the rest is regulatory sequence, repetitive DNA and material whose function is still being worked out.

questions.q: Describe the process of semi-conservative DNA replication, naming the main enzymes. Explain why one strand is synthesised continuously and the other discontinuously, and describe how the Meselson-Stahl experiment distinguished the semi-conservative model from its two rivals.
questions.solution:
**The three models that were on the table.**

**Conservative:** the parent double helix stays intact and an entirely new double helix is made alongside it.

**Semi-conservative:** the strands separate, and each templates a new partner, so every daughter molecule is half old and half new.

**Dispersive:** the DNA is broken up and old and new segments are interspersed throughout both daughter molecules.

**The process, as it actually works.**

**1. Unwinding.** **Helicase** breaks the hydrogen bonds between the bases and unwinds the double helix, forming a replication fork. **Topoisomerase** relieves the supercoiling that builds up ahead of the fork, and single-strand binding proteins keep the separated strands apart.

**2. Priming.** **Primase** lays down a short RNA primer, because DNA polymerase cannot start a chain from nothing — it can only **extend** an existing $3'$ end.

**3. Elongation.** **DNA polymerase III** adds nucleotides complementary to the template, working strictly in the $5'\to3'$ direction. It also **proofreads**, excising a mismatched base and replacing it, which is why replication is so accurate.

**4. Finishing.** **DNA polymerase I** removes the RNA primers and fills the gaps with DNA, and **ligase** seals the remaining nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone.

**Why one strand is continuous and the other is not.**

Two facts collide:

- The two strands are **antiparallel** — one runs $5'\to3'$, the other $3'\to5'$.
- DNA polymerase can add nucleotides **only to a free $3'$ end**, so it can only build in the $5'\to3'$ direction.

The fork opens in one direction. On the template running $3'\to5'$ towards the fork, the polymerase can follow the fork continuously — this is the **leading strand**, made in one unbroken piece.

On the other template the required direction of synthesis points **away** from the fork. The polymerase cannot run backwards, so it must wait for a stretch to open up, then synthesise a short piece **backwards** relative to the fork's movement, then wait again. The result is the **lagging strand**, built as a series of **Okazaki fragments** (1000 to 2000 nucleotides in prokaryotes, much shorter in eukaryotes), each needing its own primer, and joined afterwards by ligase.

So the discontinuity is not a design feature or an inefficiency — it is the **unavoidable consequence** of an antiparallel molecule copied by a one-directional enzyme.

**The Meselson-Stahl experiment (1958).**

**E. coli** was grown for many generations in medium containing the heavy nitrogen isotope $^{15}\text{N}$, so all its DNA was heavy. The cells were then transferred to ordinary $^{14}\text{N}$ medium and samples taken each generation, with the DNA separated by **caesium chloride density-gradient centrifugation** — denser DNA settles lower in the tube.

**Generation 0:** one band, at the heavy position. As expected.

**Generation 1:** one band, at **intermediate** density — every molecule half heavy and half light.

This single result **eliminates the conservative model outright**. Conservative replication would give **two** bands, one fully heavy and one fully light, and there is no intermediate band in it at all.

**Generation 2:** **two** bands, one intermediate and one light, in equal amounts.

This eliminates the **dispersive** model, which predicts a single band getting progressively lighter each generation and never splitting in two. Semi-conservative replication predicts exactly what was seen: each hybrid molecule separates into one heavy and one light strand, giving two hybrid molecules and two fully light ones.

**Why it is such a good experiment.** Neither generation alone would settle the question — generation 1 is consistent with both semi-conservative and dispersive replication. It is the **pair of results** that leaves only one model standing, and each rival is ruled out by a different observation. Taylor later confirmed the same conclusion in the broad bean using radioactive thymidine, showing it holds in eukaryotes too.
